elements.text: Drone Traffic Fingerprinting
What We Can Detect, Exploit, and Package
Sources: Christof 2021 (DJI Wi-Fi RE thesis) · Behind the Wings 2023 (DJI hijacking) · OcuSync DroneID 2026 · Detecting Drones via Encrypted Traffic Analysis 2019 · Drone Profiling 2018
The Paper's Gaps

rows: Encrypted Wi-Fi looks like any high-bandwidth client
Misses 5 GHz and OcuSync drones entirely
No direction finding or range discrimination
Cannot differentiate drone model or flight mode

elements.text: Layer 1 — 802.11 MAC Layer (ESP32 Today)
Visible from promiscuous frame headers. Zero decryption needed.

rows: Range estimate, variance for stability scoring
Biometric: small stick commands vs large video frames
Drone AP name, if not hidden

elements.text: Layer 2 — Encrypted Traffic Statistics
Survive WPA2 encryption. 90%+ accuracy from ~170 packets (820ms of traffic).

rows: No idle gaps over 200ms in active session

elements.text: Key insight: A smartphone streaming video sends ACKs both ways. A drone link is nearly one-directional. That asymmetry alone is a powerful classifier.
Layer 3 — Decrypted DJI DUML Protocol
Christof 2021: No application-layer encryption on top of WPA2. DUML payload is plaintext post-decrypt.

rows: Firm DJI identifier at payload level
Identifies operation: fly, camera, battery, OSD
Lat, lon, height, velocity, pitch/roll/yaw, flight status
Tracks all packets in one flight session
Sequential ordering, detects packet loss or injection

elements.text: Asymmetric Advantages
1. The drone cannot stop transmitting. A drone in flight requires continuous bidirectional comms. It cannot go silent without landing. The target is always emitting.
2. Video streaming is a forcing function. 1080p at 30fps requires ~4 Mbps via MTU-size frames. No consumer IoT device matches this. Phones have bidirectional ACK traffic — drones don't.
3. The protocol is deterministic. DJI DUML has fixed 0x55 delimiters, known CRC-16 Kermit, fixed field positions. Even within encrypted packets, statistical marker searches yield signatures.
4. Hardware is 1000x cheaper. $5 ESP32 captures all Layer 1-2 data. WPA2 handshake capture is a software addition. Commercial C-UAS starts at $2,000.
5. The attacker cannot spoof the profile. Changing packet sizes, timing, and directionality requires firmware modification. Consumer drones don't allow this. Only custom FPV builds could attempt it.
Proposed 5-Layer Detection Model
Rebalanced weights reduce OUI (spoofable) and elevate traffic-pattern features (unspoofable without firmware changes).
Original paper: OUI(40) + Rate(30) + Var(20) + SSID(10) = 100
Proposed: DirRatio(25) + PktSize(25) + OUI(20) + Timing(20) + Var(5) + SSID(5) = 100
FPV and Homebrew Drones — ESP32 Blind Spots
Above analysis applies to Wi-Fi drones. FPV drones use completely different RF. The ESP32 cannot see them.
FPV Drone RF Profile
Critical: An FPV drone emits NO 802.11 frames. The 5.8 GHz video link is the only passive detection vector and it requires different hardware.
Homebrew on Wi-Fi — More Detectable

Key insight: MAVLink's 1Hz heartbeat is the most reliable drone signature. Every MAVLink drone broadcasts system ID, component ID, and flight mode in plaintext every second. Any Wi-Fi sniffer can identify it with 100% certainty from a single packet.
Drones Without Remote ID
Hardest problem: FPV drone on ELRS (900 MHz FHSS) with analog 5.8 GHz video. No Wi-Fi, no BLE, no RID. Detection requires 5.8 GHz RF energy (presence only) or SDR with FHSS tracking.
Multi-Modal Detection Strategy
Minimum viable stack: one ESP32 + one $10 RTL-SDR with 5.8 GHz antenna + one HackRF. Total BOM: ~$50-150 per node.
Implementation Roadmap

rows: Packet size histogram + direction ratio. 50% weight.
Post-process PCAPs, extract telemetry and video.
TinyML classifier using all 5 traffic layers.
